# Attempt to commit a crime
## Full article
In 2026, federal appellate authority emphasized that attempts generally required specific intent. In *United States v. Castro Alavez* (9th Cir. 2026), the court reaffirmed this rule in an attempted federal drug offense.
A second defense is impossibility. However, only legal, not factual, impossibilities constitute a defense to attempt a crime. An act constitutes a legal impossibility if it is not defined by law as a crime. Keeping with the principle of legality, there cannot be a punishment. Factual impossibility is not a defense to attempt because, but for some extraneous factor unknown to the actor that prevents the crime from happening, the crime would have been completed.

**Panel:** Ryan D. Nelson, VanDyke, Douglas Russell Cole (S.D. Ohio) (authored)

**Holding:** Admission of prior similar conviction in transportation of illegal aliens trial did not violate Federal Rules of Evidence 403 or 404(b).

Border Patrol agents apprehended Alex Ruiz transporting noncitizens in southern California near the border with Mexico. The government charged Mr. Ruiz with transportation of illegal aliens in violation of 8 U.S.C. § 1324. Over Mr. Ruiz’s objection, the district court permitted the government to introduce at trial evidence that he had pleaded guilty and been convicted of having committed the same offense less than two years earlier. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that the evidence satisfied the circuit’s four-part test governing the admission of prior bad act evidence subject to Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b): (1) it tended to prove a material point—Mr. Ruiz’s knowledge that his passengers were noncitizens; (2) the prior conviction was not too remote in time; (3) Mr. Ruiz’s guilty plea and conviction sufficiently proved that the prior offense occurred; and (4) the prior offense was sufficiently similar to the instant offense, because the offenses occurred in the same region and in both cases Mr. Ruiz was the driver. The admission of the evidence did not violate Federal Rule of Evidence 403 because it was “fairly, not unfairly, prejudicial.” The court found no plain error in respect to Mr. Ruiz’s unpreserved due process and Sixth Amendment fair trial claims for essentially the same reasons.

## Nature Of The Case

This section contains the nature of the case and procedural background.

## Facts

In United States v. Cruz, 127 F. 3d 791, 795 (CA9 1997), the Ninth Circuit, following the language of an earlier case, United States v. Castro, 972 F. 2d 1107, 1112 (CA9 1992), wrote that a conspiracy terminates when ' 'there is affirmative evidence of abandonment, withdrawal, disavowal or defeat of the object of the conspiracy' ' (emphasis added).
